title: The crow in Babylon
hookLine: a crow is prized in a foreign land until a peacock arrives (Jataka 339)

cards: In the land of Baveru, the tale says, there were no birds at all. Some readers take Baveru to be Babylon. Into this birdless country sail merchants from far away, with a crow aboard their ship.
An ordinary black crow. The people of Baveru crowd the dock to see it. They have never seen anything like it, and they can't stop talking about it.

teach.h: THE CROW IN A FINE CAGE.
teach.b: First, the crow's glory. The people of Baveru praise everything about it: the gloss of its feathers, its beak, its voice. They buy it for a high price, keep it in a fine cage, and feed it meat and fruit.
For a while, a plain crow is the talk of the country.
Second, the peacock. On a later voyage, the merchants bring a peacock, trained to cry out at a snap of the fingers and dance at a clap of the hands. The people are dazzled.
It sells for far more than the crow ever did. Third, the crow forgotten.

From that day nobody brings the crow its meat and fruit. It flies off, and the tale leaves it scratching for scraps in a rubbish heap. The verse says it plainly: until the peacock came, they honored the crow.
Fourth, reading it. The crow did nothing wrong.

It never changed: a crow when they praised it, and a crow when they forgot it. It was prized because nothing else was there, and dropped the moment something brighter arrived. So the praise was never quite about the crow.
Praise that depends on there being no peacock was always borrowed. Being ordinary was never the loss; the praise was only ever a season.

how: The Pali texts name eight worldly conditions that keep the world turning: gain and loss, fame and disrepute, praise and blame, pleasure and pain. Teachers use tales like this one to show praise leaving as easily as it came.

games.why: the crow, forgotten, flies off to a rubbish heap. it was a crow all along; only the praise had changed.

practice: Sit as an ordinary person on an ordinary day, with no achievement to admire and no audience.
Feel the plain things, your weight on the seat, the air at your nose, a sound somewhere in the room, and see whether it's restful that none of it is special. Let the peacocks dance somewhere else.

wordCard.voice: Mayura. Peacock: the bird whose arrival ended a plain crow's glory in a land with no birds, in a Jataka tale. Today's word.

orig.note: Pali: mayura, peacock, the bird whose arrival ends the crow's glory.
